Quick start: annotating with FAVOR

GLOWr Package

2026-10-09

Source: vignettes/favor-annotation-quick-start.Rmd
favor-annotation-quick-start.Rmd

This vignette is the short route through annotate_favor(): when to use it, what to have ready, which settings to choose, what comes out, and how to check it. The companion vignette “Annotating genotype data with FAVOR” (vignette("favor-annotation", package = "GLOWr")) gives the evidence, the cost measurements and the matching procedure in full.

When to use annotate_favor()

Use annotate_favor() when you have variants on GRCh38 and need FAVOR’s functional annotation attached to them: a cohort GDS that a GLOW scan (the variant-set association method of this package, run by the GLOWpipeline package) or STAARpipeline will read, or a table of variants for training GLOWr’s variant-importance score (PI), which weights the variants in a scan. The function reads the FAVOR database from your own disk, finds the database row for each variant, and returns the annotation together with a record of how each variant was matched. With output_agds it also writes the annotated GDS (an aGDS) in the layout that GLOW’s scans and STAARpipeline read.

FAVOR keys every variant by CHR-POS-REF-ALT, where REF is the base the reference genome carries. match_method = "exact" looks the key up exactly as given, so it annotates only the variants whose alleles already follow that convention. Sequencing data in VCF form do. Genotyping-chip data usually do not, because a PLINK file carries each probe’s two alleles in the probe’s own order and on the probe’s strand. Beyond the exact lookup, annotate_favor() adds four things:

  • Flexible allele matching, with a check. For a chip SNV it also tries the key with the alleles swapped, with both complemented, and with both, and it records which form found the row (match_tier). It then compares the input’s rsID with the matched row’s (rsid_check) and by default withholds a rewritten match that the rsID contradicts. Your genotype file is never changed. On an ALS case-control data set genotyped on an Illumina array, about 48,000 samples and 413,528 variants, the allele labeled REF was the reference base for 36% of the variants, so exact matching would have annotated that share only. Flexible matching found a row for all of them, and the chip’s rsID agreed with the FAVOR row’s for 99.89% of the 265,462 matches found by a rewritten key.

  • Variants without alleles. annotate_favor() annotates a key of the form CHR-POS-NA-NA, common in literature-curated variant lists, from the SNV rows at the position, and labels it position_only, so you know which values are aggregates.

  • Both database releases, read locally. The FAVOR v1 CSV chunks and the FAVOR 2.0 Parquet files are both read, and the provenance of the annotation (database files, settings, outcome counts, date) is written into the aGDS.

  • Throughput for a whole cohort. With FAVOR 2.0, the 22 autosomes of that chip data set took 2,333 seconds in total, and chromosome 22 of the 1000 Genomes high-coverage sequencing panel (3,202 samples, 1,066,557 variants) took 205 seconds. The companion vignette’s cost table gives time and peak memory for both database routes.

What you need

annotate_favor() needs these ready before the call: variants on GRCh38 in one of three forms, the FAVOR database on disk, two R packages, rsIDs when the input is chip data, and disk space for the aGDS.

Need Details
Variants on GRCh38 FAVOR’s positions are GRCh38. Convert the positions first if your data are on another build.
The variants, in one of three forms A GDS file path (one chromosome per call, the usual form for a cohort). A data frame with a VarInfo column of CHR-POS-REF-ALT keys and, optionally, an rsID column. The case or control object from prepare_PI_case_data() or prepare_PI_control_data().
The FAVOR database on disk Obtained from the FAVOR team, since GLOWr does not redistribute it. Either the v1 CSV chunk directory of chr<N>_<K>.csv files (its split table FAVORdatabase_chrsplit.csv is bundled with GLOWr), or the FAVOR 2.0 directory of chromosome_<N>.parquet files.
R packages GLOWr. SeqArray for GDS input and aGDS output. arrow for the Parquet files. The optional command-line tool xsv speeds up the CSV route. Without it the chunks are read with data.table::fread().
rsIDs in the input, for chip data A GDS made with SeqArray::seqBED2GDS() carries column 2 of the .bim as annotation/id. That is the evidence the rsID check reads, so keep it.
Disk space The aGDS is a copy of the input GDS plus the annotation nodes.

Which settings to choose

The call for one chromosome of chip data is one line per argument. Replace the three paths with your own. The example does not create them.

res <- annotate_favor(
  variants      = "genotypes/chr22.gds",          # your GDS, one chromosome
  favor_db_path = "/path/to/FAVOR2.0",            # the FAVOR 2.0 directory, or the v1 chunk directory
  match_method  = "flexible",                     # "exact" for sequencing data in the reference convention
  favor_release = "FAVOR 2.0, downloaded 2026",   # a free-text label recorded in the aGDS provenance
  output_agds   = "genotypes_favor/chr22.gds",    # the annotated GDS for the scans
  output_csv    = "genotypes_favor/chr22.csv")    # the returned table on disk, for the record

The arguments that decide what happens:

Argument Choose Why
match_method "flexible" for chip data. "exact" for sequencing data whose alleles follow the reference convention. Exact matching tries the key as given only. Flexible matching adds the three rewritten keys for SNVs. Indels match by the exact key under both.
rsid_policy Leave the default "require" for an annotation you will analyze. "record" to see what the lookup alone finds. Under "require" a rewritten match whose rsID differs from the row’s, or whose row carries no rsID, is withheld as rsid_conflict. Exact matches, and inputs without rsIDs, are never withheld.
features Leave the default unless you need fewer fields. The default is the 30 fields of the FAVOR Essential Database: 20 numeric scores and 10 categorical fields, among them the GENCODE and MetaSVM fields the built-in coding masks read. FAVOR 2.0 lacks four older score versions, so the default yields 26 fields there.
output_agds, update_gds, output_csv output_agds for a new annotated file. update_gds = TRUE to write the annotation into the input GDS instead. output_csv for the table. See the next section.
variant_filter list(chr = "22"), or list(chr = "22", start = 1e6, end = 5e6), to restrict a call. One call per chromosome is the natural unit.
favor_db_format Leave "auto". The layout is detected from the directory. A directory holding both layouts, or neither, is an error, and you then name the format.
na_allele_method "average" (the default) or "first". Only for CHR-POS-NA-NA keys. Resolve the alleles first when you can.
na_handling Leave "keep". "zero" replaces a missing numeric value with 0. "drop" removes rows with any missing annotation from the table and the CSV. Neither changes the matching outcome.

What you get

One call to annotate_favor() can produce up to three things: the returned table for inspection, a CSV copy for the record, and an annotated GDS for the scans of GLOW and STAARpipeline. The table says which is for auditing and which for analysis.

Output What it is Use it for
res, the returned data frame The input columns (for a GDS also variant_id and rsID), one column per annotation feature, and the three records match_tier, favor_key and rsid_check. Inspecting and auditing the matching. The input of the variant-importance training functions.
output_csv The same table written to disk. The record you keep. With the returned table, the only place favor_key is stored.
output_agds, or the input GDS under update_gds = TRUE A copy of the input GDS plus one node per feature under annotation/info/FunctionalAnnotation, the outcome as annotation/info/favor_match_tier, the check as annotation/info/favor_rsid_check, and the provenance as attributes of the FunctionalAnnotation folder. The downstream analyses: GLOW’s gene, window and coding scans, and STAARpipeline.

favor_key is the CHR-POS-REF-ALT of the FAVOR row that supplied the annotation, or of the row withheld under rsid_conflict. The aGDS does not store it, so keep the returned table or request output_csv when you need the keys.

How to know it worked

Two checks confirm that the call worked: the outcome counts in the returned table, and the same counts read back from the aGDS. Read the outcome table first:

table(res$match_tier)
table(res$rsid_check)

  • On chip data under flexible matching, expect the four key forms (exact, swapped, flipped, flipped_swapped), a small number of rsid_conflict, and the reasons a key was not found. On the chip data set above, the default policy withheld 289 rewritten matches, about one in a thousand.

  • On sequencing data under exact matching, expect exact and the reasons a key was not found: uncovered (FAVOR has no row at the position), unmatched_alt (the position is covered and the reference base agrees, but FAVOR has no row for that allele pair) and unmatched_ref (the input’s REF is not the reference base).

  • rsid_check is mostly same on chip data. It is chip_none throughout when the input carries no rsIDs, the usual case for sequencing data, and nothing is then withheld.

  • A large unmatched_ref share on chip data under exact matching means the alleles do not follow the reference convention. Rerun with match_method = "flexible".

Then confirm that the aGDS carries the annotation. The counts must equal those of res:

g <- SeqArray::seqOpen("genotypes_favor/chr22.gds")
table(SeqArray::seqGetData(g, "annotation/info/favor_match_tier"))
table(SeqArray::seqGetData(g, "annotation/info/favor_rsid_check"))
fa <- gdsfmt::index.gdsn(g, "annotation/info/FunctionalAnnotation")
gdsfmt::ls.gdsn(fa)                 # one node per annotation feature
str(gdsfmt::get.attr.gdsn(fa))      # the provenance: database files, settings, counts, date
SeqArray::seqClose(g)

Where to read more

Three places carry more than this quick start does:

  • vignette("favor-annotation", package = "GLOWr"): the evidence, the cost table, the two database layouts, where each record lives, and the optional alignment of chip alleles before conversion. Its appendices give every value of match_tier and rsid_check (A), the keys without alleles (B), and a worked example on a made-up database that you can run (C).

  • ?annotate_favor: every argument and its default.

  • The GLOWanalyses workflow templates run annotate_favor() per chromosome as a job array (00-data-prep/annotate-favor.R with slurm/run-annotate-favor.sh) and write a provenance snapshot beside the output.
